quick: 150 mg IM once daily for 3 days
Avoid in 1st trimester; use in severe malaria if needed
Limited data; use if clearly needed
summary: Arteether (beta-arteether/Artemotil) is a lipid-soluble artemisinin derivative given by deep intramuscular injection for severe/complicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including cerebral malaria, especially where parenteral artesunate is unavailable. A typical adult course is 150 mg IM once daily for 3 days. It is not FDA-approved.
indications: Severe and complicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (including cerebral malaria)
Multidrug-resistant falciparum malaria where parenteral therapy is required

dosage.d: 150 mg by deep IM injection once daily for 3 days
dosage.n: Follow with a full oral ACT course once able to tolerate orally

dosage.d: Approx 4.8 mg/kg total over 3 days (per WHO/manufacturer guidance)
dosage.n: Use age/weight-appropriate dosing under specialist care

admin: Give by deep intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
Reserve for severe/complicated malaria requiring parenteral therapy
Always follow with a complete oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) to prevent recrudescence
Do not use as monotherapy for uncomplicated malaria
Monitor for neurological and cardiac effects during therapy
moa: Like other artemisinins, arteether contains an endoperoxide bridge that is cleaved by heme iron within the parasite, generating reactive free radicals and carbon-centered radicals that alkylate parasite proteins and damage membranes. This produces rapid killing of asexual blood-stage Plasmodium parasites.

relative: First trimester of pregnancy (unless severe malaria mandates treatment)

preg: Avoid in the first trimester unless the benefit in severe, life-threatening malaria outweighs risk; artemisinins are used in 2nd/3rd trimester severe malaria when alternatives are inadequate. Specialist guidance advised.
lact: Limited data on excretion in breast milk; use only if clearly needed for severe maternal malaria.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; data are limited.

major: Other QT-prolonging antimalarials (e.g. quinine, halofantrine) - additive cardiac risk
moderate: CYP-inducing/inhibiting drugs - may alter artemisinin metabolism
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently affect liver enzymes and reticulocyte counts.

serious: Neurotoxicity (gait/balance disturbance reported in animal studies at high doses)

monitoring: Neurological examination during and after therapy
ECG if cardiac risk factors or QT-prolonging co-medication
Hemoglobin for delayed hemolysis after artemisinin therapy
counsel: This injection treats severe malaria - you must also complete the follow-on oral tablets
Report any unusual weakness, balance problems or palpitations
Finish the entire follow-on treatment course to prevent relapse
Watch for delayed tiredness or pallor after recovery (possible delayed anemia)
Attend follow-up to confirm the malaria has cleared
pk: Slow IM absorption; peak over several hours
Store as per manufacturer; protect from light
pearls: Lipophilic artemisinin given as a deep IM depot - useful where IV artesunate is unavailable
Always follow parenteral artemisinin with a full oral ACT to prevent recrudescence
Never use as monotherapy for uncomplicated malaria (resistance risk)
Watch for post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis in the weeks after treatment
missed: Doses are given once daily for 3 days under medical supervision; if a scheduled dose is delayed, give it as soon as possible and continue the course, then complete the follow-on oral ACT.
overdose: Experience is limited; overdose may increase risk of neurological and cardiac effects. Management is supportive with cardiac and neurological monitoring; there is no specific antidote.
